description: Standardised procedures, randomisation, counterbalancing, reliability, validity and BPS ethics.
content_html:
Designing Research That Works

Collecting data is only valuable if the data accurately reflects what you intended to measure. Two fundamental concepts underpin the quality of any psychological study: reliability and validity. Beyond quality, research involving human participants also carries ethical responsibilities — and in the UK, these are set out by the British Psychological Society (BPS).

Standardised Procedures

A key way to improve reliability is to use standardised procedures. This means every participant experiences exactly the same conditions: the same instructions, the same environment, the same timing, the same stimuli. Without standardisation, differences between participants’ performance could reflect differences in how the study was conducted rather than genuine variation in the variable being measured.

Standardised instructions to participants are a core part of this. Written instructions ensure that every participant receives identical information before the study begins. The researcher delivers the same briefing — or participants read the same text — regardless of who is conducting the session. This also means that if another researcher wants to replicate the study, they can follow the same procedure and expect comparable results.

Key Fact

Reliability = consistency (getting the same result each time the study is run under the same conditions). Validity = accuracy (measuring what you actually intend to measure, in a way that reflects real behaviour). A study can be reliable without being valid: for example, a memory test that consistently scores the same people highly may be measuring intelligence rather than memory.

Randomisation and Allocation to Conditions

Randomisation refers to using chance to allocate participants to conditions. In an independent groups design, random allocation means each participant has an equal chance of being placed in condition A or condition B. This controls for individual differences between conditions — it reduces the risk that one group is systematically different from the other in a way that could affect results.

Randomisation can also be used to determine the order in which stimuli are presented (for example, if a researcher is testing memory for a list of words, the order in which the words appear should be randomised to prevent order from affecting which words are recalled).

Counterbalancing is used in repeated measures designs to reduce order effects. When the same participants take part in multiple conditions, there is a risk that their performance in later conditions is affected by having already done earlier ones — either improved by practice or reduced by fatigue. Counterbalancing divides participants so that half do condition A then condition B (AB order), and the other half do condition B then condition A (BA order). If any order effect exists, it is spread equally across both conditions and cancels out.

Counterbalancing is distinct from randomisation of stimuli. It specifically addresses the sequence of experimental conditions when participants take part in all of them.

Extraneous Variables and Controlling Them

Any variable that could affect the dependent variable other than the independent variable is an extraneous variable. If not controlled, extraneous variables become confounding variables — they provide an alternative explanation for any difference found between conditions. Researchers control extraneous variables through standardised procedures, random allocation, controlled settings, and matched pairs or repeated measures designs.

Reliability and Validity in Research Planning

When planning research, psychologists consider reliability and validity at every stage. Sampling methods affect external validity (how well results generalise to the target population) — a biased sample reduces it. Experimental designs affect internal validity — poor control of extraneous variables means the IV may not be the real cause of any difference found. Quantitative and qualitative methods differ in their reliability and validity trade-offs: quantitative data is more reliable and easier to compare, but may miss the depth and meaning of experience; qualitative data captures richer detail but is harder to replicate consistently.

Psychological research involves human participants, which creates ethical responsibilities. The BPS sets out guidelines that researchers must follow. Key ethical issues include informed consent — participants must be told what the study involves and agree to take part freely, without pressure. They have the right to withdraw at any point without penalty.

Confidentiality means that participants’ personal data must be kept private and not shared without consent. Protection from harm requires researchers to ensure no lasting physical or psychological damage results from participation. After the study, a debrief must be provided: participants are told the full purpose of the study and are given the chance to ask questions or withdraw their data.

Where deception has been used (withholding the true purpose to prevent demand characteristics), the debrief is especially important. Deception should only be used if it is unavoidable and it must not cause participants lasting distress. The right to withdraw data after the study is part of the debrief process.

Key Fact

The BPS ethical guidelines require: informed consent (explain study, get agreement), right to withdraw (can leave at any time, no penalty), confidentiality (data kept anonymous), protection from harm (no lasting physical or psychological damage), and debrief (full explanation after the study, option to withdraw data).
exam_tip_html: Ethical questions are regularly lost marks because students name the issues without explaining how a researcher would deal with them. For each issue — informed consent, right to withdraw, confidentiality, protection from harm, debrief — state the issue and then explain the practical step a researcher takes to address it. ‘The researcher should get consent’ is incomplete; ‘The researcher should provide a written information sheet and obtain signed consent before the study begins’ is complete. Always pair issue with solution.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Standardised procedures ensure every participant experiences the same conditions, improving reliability. Randomisation reduces bias in allocation; counterbalancing reduces order effects in repeated measures designs.
  • Reliability is consistency; validity is whether you are measuring what you claim to measure. Both must be considered when planning sampling, experimental designs and research methods.
  • BPS ethical guidelines require informed consent, right to withdraw, confidentiality, protection from harm and a debrief. Each issue must be paired with a practical solution in exam answers.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes 'standardised procedures' in psychological research?
A) Using the same participants across all conditions
B) Ensuring every participant experiences the same conditions and instructions
C) Using a random sample from the target population
D) Comparing results to a standardised population norm
practice_questions.marks: B) Ensuring every participant experiences the same conditions and instructions [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define what is meant by 'validity' in psychological research.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'The extent to which a study measures what it claims to measure and whether findings can be applied beyond the study context.' — both elements present.
Secure: Core idea correct — measures what it claims to measure and some reference to generalisability.
Developing: Confuses reliability and validity, or mentions only one aspect without the other.
Emerging: Incorrect or incomplete definition.

practice_questions.text: Describe how counterbalancing is used to reduce order effects in a repeated measures design.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- In a repeated measures design, the same participants complete all conditions, creating a risk of order effects (practice or fatigue).
- Counterbalancing: half the participants complete condition A then B; the other half complete B then A.
- This spreads any order effect equally across both conditions so it does not bias one condition more than the other.
Mastering: What it is, how it is done, and why it works — all clear.
Secure: Two of three elements.
Developing: Mentions counterbalancing and order effects without explaining the mechanism.
Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: A researcher studying stress tells participants the study is about 'reaction times'. After the study, she explains its true purpose and gives participants the chance to withdraw their data. Identify two ethical issues shown in this scenario and explain how each was dealt with.
practice_questions.marks:
Issue 1: Deception — participants were not told the true purpose (told it was about reaction times). Dealt with: debrief after the study disclosed the real purpose.
Issue 2: Right to withdraw data — participants were given the opportunity to withdraw their data after the study ended.
(Credit also: protection from harm if stress is discussed; informed consent was partly compromised by deception.)
Mastering: Two issues identified and dealt with, both linked to the scenario.
Secure: Two issues, one linked to scenario.
Developing: One issue identified and dealt with.
Emerging: One issue named only.

practice_questions.text: Describe the ethical guidelines set out by the British Psychological Society for research with human participants.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should cover at least four of:
- Informed consent: participants must be told what the study involves and agree freely.
- Right to withdraw: participants can leave at any time without penalty.
- Confidentiality: personal data kept private; participants cannot be identified from published results.
- Protection from harm: no lasting physical or psychological damage.
- Debrief: full explanation of the study's purpose after completion; option to withdraw data.
- Deception: only used when unavoidable; must be addressed in debrief.
Mastering: Four or more issues described with how each is addressed.
Secure: Three issues described with solutions.
Developing: Two issues named and dealt with.
Emerging: Two issues named without solutions.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the importance of standardised procedures, randomisation and counterbalancing in planning psychological research.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1):
- Standardised procedures: fixed instructions and conditions for all participants; ensures consistency; enables replication.
- Randomisation: chance allocation of participants to conditions; reduces systematic bias; controls individual differences between groups.
- Counterbalancing: in repeated measures designs, AB order for half, BA for the other half; reduces order effects (practice, fatigue).
- All three increase reliability and/or validity of the study.

Evaluation (AO3):
- Strength of standardisation: increases reliability — same procedure can be replicated to check results.
- Limitation: over-standardised procedures may reduce ecological validity if conditions become too artificial.
- Strength of randomisation: controls individual differences between groups, improving internal validity.
- Limitation: random allocation does not guarantee equal groups, especially with small samples.
- Strength of counterbalancing: effectively reduces order effects without requiring a separate group.
- Limitation: even with counterbalancing, some tasks are impossible to counterbalance (e.g. if order exposure permanently changes behaviour).

Mastering: All three described accurately with elaborated evaluations.
Secure: All three described, two evaluations.
Developing: Two topics described, one evaluation.
Emerging: One topic, little evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the purpose of counterbalancing in a repeated measures design?
options: To randomly assign participants to conditions
To ensure all participants complete the same number of trials
To control for order effects by varying the sequence of conditions
To match participants on a relevant variable before the study

knowledge_checks.q: Which BPS ethical principle requires that participants are told the full purpose of the study after it has ended?
The extent to which a study produces consistent results when repeated under the same conditions is called _____.
Using chance to allocate participants to conditions in order to reduce researcher bias is called _____.
Match each ethical issue to how it is dealt with:
right: Provide an information sheet; obtain agreement before the study
Use a full debrief to explain the true purpose after the study
Ensure no lasting physical or psychological damage from participation

flashcard_questions.a: Fixed conditions and instructions identical for every participant, ensuring consistency and replicability.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the purpose of randomisation in an experiment?
flashcard_questions.a: To allocate participants to conditions by chance, reducing systematic bias.

flashcard_questions.q: What is counterbalancing and when is it used?
flashcard_questions.a: Half of participants do condition A then B; the other half do B then A — used in repeated measures to control order effects.

flashcard_questions.q: What is reliability in psychological research?
flashcard_questions.a: The extent to which a study produces consistent results when repeated under the same conditions.

flashcard_questions.q: What is validity in psychological research?
flashcard_questions.a: The extent to which a study measures what it claims to measure.

flashcard_questions.q: What is informed consent in research ethics?
flashcard_questions.a: Participants are told the purpose and procedure of the study and agree freely before taking part.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the right to withdraw in research ethics?
flashcard_questions.a: Participants can leave the study at any time without penalty or giving a reason.

flashcard_questions.q: What is confidentiality in research ethics?
flashcard_questions.a: Participants' personal data is kept private so they cannot be identified from results.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a debrief in psychological research?
flashcard_questions.a: A session after the study explaining its true purpose and giving participants the option to withdraw data.
An extraneous variable that varies systematically with the IV, providing an alternative explanation for results.

glossary_terms.definition: The extent to which a study produces consistent results when repeated under the same conditions.
The extent to which a study measures what it claims to measure and whether findings can be generalised beyond the study setting.
The professional body for psychology in the UK that sets ethical standards for research involving human participants.
Fixed procedures and instructions that are the same for every participant in a study, ensuring consistency and allowing the study to be replicated.
The use of chance procedures (such as random number tables or drawing lots) to allocate participants to conditions, reducing researcher bias.
A technique used in repeated measures designs to control for order effects by ensuring that half the participants complete conditions in one order and the other half in the reverse order.
An extraneous variable that has not been controlled and that systematically varies with the independent variable, threatening the validity of the study.
Providing participants with a clear account of the purpose and procedures of a study before they agree to take part, so that agreement is genuinely informed.
The entitlement of participants to stop taking part in a study at any time, without penalty or having to give a reason.
Keeping participants' personal information and responses private, so that individuals cannot be identified from the data.
Protection from harm — participants must not be exposed to physical or psychological risks greater than those encountered in everyday life.
A session after the study ends in which participants are fully informed of the true purpose of the research and given the opportunity to ask questions or withdraw their data.
Deliberately withholding the true purpose of a study from participants to prevent it affecting their behaviour.

hero_image_caption: Ethical research protects participants through consent, confidentiality and debriefing.
